title: Load Balancing
summary: Send traffic to healthy instances, keep sessions safe when one disappears and make sure the load balancer can survive failures too.
body:
A load balancer does not create capacity; it makes existing capacity usable and lets the service survive a failed instance. Before choosing an algorithm, ask whether the backends are interchangeable and what happens when one disappears.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    C["Clients"] --> DNS["DNS name of the balancer"]
    DNS --> LBA["Balancer node, zone A"]
    DNS --> LBB["Balancer node, zone B"]
    LBA --> A1["App A1"]
    LBA --> B1["App B1"]
    LBB --> A1
    LBB --> B1
    A1 --> R[("Shared session store")]
    B1 --> R
```

Clients resolve one name that maps to balancer nodes in two zones, and each node can forward to healthy instances in either zone. Because sessions live in a shared store, any instance can serve any user, so a failed instance or a failed zone reduces capacity instead of ending sessions.

## Choose the layer

| Layer | Sees | Good fit | Limitation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| L4 (TCP/UDP) | IP, port, connection | Fast pass-through, TLS terminated at the app | Cannot route by URL, header or cookie |
| L7 (HTTP) | Method, path, headers | /images to a media service, auth and canary routing | Terminates HTTP/TLS and adds processing and configuration |

An AWS Network Load Balancer is an L4 example; an Application Load Balancer, NGINX or Envoy can make L7 decisions. L4 routing sees connections, not necessarily requests: one HTTP/2 connection may carry many concurrent requests. L7 is useful when request-aware routing matters, not automatically better for every workload.

## Choose a routing policy

- **Round robin** is fine when requests cost about the same and instances have similar capacity. Weighted round robin handles unequal instance sizes.
- **Least connections** helps when connection lifetimes differ, but an idle connection and a busy request are not the same load. Least outstanding requests or observed latency may be a better signal for HTTP.
- **Consistent hashing** on a stable key can preserve cache locality. It can also make a hot customer overload one instance; hashing distributes keys, not equal work.

For 1,000 RPS spread across four equivalent instances, start with round robin and measure per-node queue time and error rate. Do not add clever routing to compensate for a slow database shared by all four.

## Health and failure

A TCP-open check proves only that a port accepts connections. Use a readiness endpoint that checks whether the instance can serve traffic, with a separate liveness check for restarting a stuck process. Probe every few seconds, require multiple failures before eviction, and drain existing connections on deploy. Avoid a readiness check that makes every backend go unhealthy when a shared optional dependency hiccups. Bound retries: retrying every failed request across all instances can turn a small failure into an overload.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant LB as Load balancer
    participant N as Instance 3
    participant D as Deployer
    loop every 5 s
        LB->>N: GET /ready
        N-->>LB: 200 OK
    end
    D->>N: Begin graceful shutdown
    N-->>LB: GET /ready now returns 503
    Note over LB: After 2 failed probes, stop sending new requests
    N->>N: Finish in-flight requests
    D->>N: Stop process after drain timeout
```

During a deploy, the instance fails its own readiness check first, so the balancer stops routing new requests to it while existing requests complete. Only after the drain timeout does the process exit. Skipping this order produces a burst of connection resets on every release.

The load balancer is also a failure domain. Managed multi-zone balancers or redundant proxy instances with independent routing remove a single proxy box as the single point of failure; test failover, not just backend eviction.

## Why sticky sessions are usually the wrong fix

Cookie- or IP-based affinity keeps a user's session on one machine, but losing that machine loses the session; IP affinity also collapses many users behind a NAT. Externalize session state to Redis or use appropriately scoped signed tokens, then any healthy instance can take the next request. Affinity can still help cache locality or a stateful protocol, but name its failure behavior explicitly.

## How to answer this in an interview

> At 1,000 RPS, I would start with four stateless application instances across two zones behind a managed L7 balancer, use round robin, probe readiness every 5 seconds and drain connections before removing a node. Sessions live in Redis, so losing one instance should only reduce capacity by about 25%.

## Further reading

- [Envoy documentation: Load balancing](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/load_balancing) describes L7 policies, health checking and outlier detection.
- [AWS Elastic Load Balancing documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/) compares network (L4) and application (L7) load balancers.
keyTakeaways: L4 routes connections; L7 can make HTTP-aware decisions but adds termination and processing.
Routing algorithms balance different signals; hashing can create hot spots despite even key counts.
Readiness, draining and bounded retries matter as much as the routing algorithm.
Stateless sessions and redundant balancers make instance and balancer failures survivable.
